mcqs.stem: Best guess: a U.S. corporation opens a sales office in France that loses money in its first year. If the office is a branch rather than a French subsidiary, what happens to the loss?

choices.explanation: That describes a subsidiary, a separate taxpayer.

choices.text: It is deducted on the U.S. return
choices.explanation: Correct. A branch is part of the U.S. corporation, so its loss flows into the U.S. return.

choices.text: It becomes a foreign tax credit
choices.explanation: A loss is a deduction, not a credit.

choices.text: It is disallowed by the U.S.

mcqs.explanation: A branch's income and losses are part of the U.S. corporation's return.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation has worldwide taxable income of $1,000,000, including $300,000 of foreign-source taxable income, and U.S. tax before credits of $210,000. It paid $50,000 of foreign income tax. What foreign tax credit is allowed?

choices.explanation: That is the limit; the credit cannot exceed the foreign tax paid.
The credit is limited to U.S. tax on foreign-source income.
Correct. The limit is 210,000 × 300,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 63,000; foreign tax paid (50,000) is lower.
This multiplies the foreign tax by the foreign-source share.

mcqs.explanation: Credit = lesser of foreign taxes paid or U.S. tax × foreign-source ÷ worldwide taxable income.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation receives interest on a loan to a French company and dividends from a U.S. corporation. How is each sourced?

choices.explanation: Correct. Interest and dividends are sourced by the residence of the payer.
Interest is sourced by the payer's residence, not the recipient's.
Dividends from a domestic corporation are U.S.-source.
Both are sourced by the payer; this reverses them.

mcqs.explanation: Interest and dividend income are sourced by the residence of the payer.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. engineer employed by a U.S. company spends three months working in Brazil on a client project and is paid $60,000 for that work by the U.S. company. Where is the $60,000 sourced?

choices.explanation: Compensation is sourced where the services are performed, not by the payer.

choices.text: Brazil, where the work was done
choices.explanation: Correct. Compensation for personal services is sourced where the services are performed.
The worker's residence does not determine the source of compensation.
The services were all performed in Brazil.

mcqs.explanation: Personal services income is sourced where the services are performed.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. manufacturer buys inventory in Mexico and resells it to customers in Canada, with title passing in Canada. Where is the income from the sales sourced?

choices.explanation: Purchased inventory is sourced where title passes, not by residence.
The place of purchase does not determine source.
Correct. Income from the sale of purchased inventory is sourced where title passes.

mcqs.explanation: Purchased inventory: title-passage rule. Produced inventory: where the production occurs.

mcqs.stem: A foreign corporation with no U.S. trade or business receives $100,000 of dividends from a U.S. corporation. No treaty applies. How is the income taxed?

choices.explanation: Net-basis tax at regular rates applies to effectively connected income, not passive FDAP income.

choices.text: It is exempt from U.S. tax
choices.explanation: U.S.-source FDAP income of a foreign person is taxable.

choices.text: It is taxed only when repatriated
choices.explanation: The tax is collected at the time of payment.
Correct. U.S.-source FDAP income is taxed at 30% of the gross amount, collected by withholding, absent a treaty.

mcqs.explanation: FDAP income not connected with a U.S. business: 30% gross withholding (§§881, 1442), often reduced by treaty.

mcqs.stem: A German company sells machines to U.S. customers. Which arrangement is most likely to create a U.S. permanent establishment under a typical treaty?

choices.text: A U.S. agent who signs its contracts
choices.explanation: Correct. A dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts on the company's behalf creates a permanent establishment.
Selling into the U.S. without a presence creates no permanent establishment.

choices.text: A U.S. warehouse used only for storage
choices.explanation: Storage alone is a preparatory or auxiliary activity.
An independent agent acting in the ordinary course of its business is not a permanent establishment.

mcqs.explanation: A permanent establishment is a fixed place of business or a dependent agent that habitually concludes contracts; auxiliary activities are excluded.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation expects its new foreign operation to lose money for three years. Which structure lets it use those losses against U.S. income?

choices.explanation: A foreign subsidiary is a separate taxpayer; its losses stay abroad.
Correct. A branch is part of the U.S. corporation, so its losses reduce U.S. taxable income.
A CFC is a foreign subsidiary; its losses do not flow to the parent.

choices.text: Either structure; the choice is irrelevant
choices.explanation: Only the branch passes losses through.

mcqs.explanation: Start-up losses favor a branch; later profits taxed at lower foreign rates may favor a subsidiary.

mcqs.stem: Five unrelated U.S. corporations each own 11% of the voting stock of a foreign corporation; foreign persons own the rest. Is the foreign corporation a CFC?

choices.text: No — no single owner has control
choices.explanation: CFC status looks at all U.S. shareholders together.
Correct. Each owns at least 10%, so each is a U.S. shareholder; together they own 55%, more than 50%.

choices.text: Yes — any U.S. ownership makes it one
choices.explanation: Owners below 10% are not counted, and the total must exceed 50%.

mcqs.explanation: CFC: more than 50% of vote or value owned by U.S. shareholders, each owning at least 10%.

mcqs.stem: What is the main consequence for a U.S. shareholder of a CFC that earns Subpart F income?

choices.text: The CFC pays U.S. tax at 21% directly
choices.explanation: The U.S. shareholder, not the CFC, is taxed.

choices.text: The income is exempt until sold
choices.explanation: Subpart F income is taxed currently.
Withholding applies to FDAP paid to foreign persons.

choices.text: It is taxed on its share as earned
choices.explanation: Correct. Subpart F requires U.S. shareholders to include their pro rata share currently.

mcqs.explanation: Subpart F (and GILTI) are anti-deferral regimes: U.S. shareholders include CFC income currently.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation has worldwide taxable income of $4,000,000, including $1,000,000 of foreign-source taxable income, and U.S. tax before credits of $840,000. It paid $300,000 of foreign tax. What is its excess foreign tax credit?

choices.explanation: That is the credit allowed, not the excess.
The foreign tax paid exceeds the limit.
This uses 25% of the foreign tax instead of the limit formula.

mcqs.explanation: Excess credit = foreign taxes paid − FTC limit.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation has $900,000 of gross income: $600,000 U.S.-source and $300,000 foreign-source. It has $150,000 of expenses definitely related to the foreign income and $200,000 of general expenses apportioned by gross income. What is its foreign-source taxable income?

choices.explanation: This omits the apportioned share of general expenses.
This apportions half of the general expenses instead of one-third.
Deductions must be allocated and apportioned to foreign-source income.

mcqs.explanation: Allocate definitely related expenses first, then apportion the rest on a reasonable basis.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation owns 30% of a foreign corporation (not a CFC) and receives a dividend paid out of the foreign corporation's foreign earnings. What deduction may apply?

choices.explanation: The 50% and 65% DRDs apply to dividends from domestic corporations.

choices.text: A foreign tax credit for all taxes
choices.explanation: A deduction, not a credit, is the key relief here; §245A dividends do not carry a deemed-paid credit.
Correct. §245A allows a 100% deduction for the foreign-source portion of dividends from a 10%-owned foreign corporation (holding period met).

choices.text: None; foreign dividends are fully taxed
choices.explanation: §245A provides a participation exemption for 10% corporate shareholders.

mcqs.explanation: §245A: a 100% DRD for the foreign-source portion of dividends from specified 10%-owned foreign corporations.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. parent sells goods to its foreign subsidiary at prices below what unrelated parties would pay. Which rule lets the IRS adjust the price?

choices.explanation: Correct. The IRS may reallocate income between related parties.
That limits the foreign tax credit.

mcqs.explanation: §482 lets the IRS allocate income among related parties to reflect arm's-length pricing.

mcqs.stem: For 2025, the foreign earned income exclusion is $130,000. A U.S. citizen works in London for 340 days of the year and earns $150,000. How much may she exclude?

choices.explanation: Correct. She meets the physical presence test.

mcqs.explanation: A taxpayer present in foreign countries at least 330 full days in 12 months may exclude foreign earned income up to the annual limit.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation's creditable foreign taxes exceed its FTC limitation this year. What happens to the excess?

choices.explanation: Correct. Excess FTCs carry back 1 and forward 10.

mcqs.explanation: §904(c): excess foreign tax credits carry back 1 year and forward 10 years.

mcqs.stem: A foreign national was in the U.S. 120 days this year, 120 days last year and 180 days the year before. Is she a U.S. resident under the substantial presence test?

choices.text: No, she has under 183 days this year
Yes, she has 420 days in total

mcqs.explanation: Substantial presence: at least 31 days this year and 183 weighted days (all current, 1/3 prior, 1/6 second prior).

mcqs.stem: A CFC buys goods from its U.S. parent and resells them to customers outside its own country. What is the income?

choices.explanation: Correct. A type of Subpart F income.

mcqs.explanation: Foreign base company sales income arises when a CFC buys from or sells to related parties, for goods made and sold outside its country.

mcqs.stem: A foreign investor in a treaty country receives U.S. dividends. How can she claim the treaty rate instead of 30%?

choices.text: Give the payer a Form W-8BEN
choices.explanation: Correct. It certifies foreign status and treaty eligibility.

mcqs.explanation: Foreign individuals claim treaty benefits by giving Form W-8BEN to the withholding agent.

mcqs.stem: In applying the FTC limitation, interest from foreign bonds held for investment falls in which category?
mcqs.explanation: The FTC limitation is computed separately for categories such as passive and general income.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation owns 15% of a foreign corporation for 200 days and receives a dividend. Does the §245A DRD apply?

choices.explanation: Correct. More than 365 days are required.
That isn't what the rule says.

mcqs.explanation: §245A requires 10% ownership and a holding period of more than 365 days in a 731-day window.

mcqs.stem: How is a foreign corporation's effectively connected income from a U.S. branch taxed?

choices.explanation: Correct. Net ECI at regular rates.

choices.text: Not at all in the U.S.
choices.explanation: ECI is taxed in the U.S.

mcqs.explanation: Net ECI is taxed at regular corporate rates, and the branch profits tax may apply to repatriated earnings.

mcqs.stem: A nonresident alien owns a U.S. rental property and wants to be taxed on net income rather than 30% of gross rents. What may she do?

choices.text: Transfer it to a C corporation

mcqs.explanation: A nonresident alien may elect under §871(d) to treat U.S. real property income as ECI, taxed on a net basis.

mcqs.stem: A dual resident has a permanent home in both countries. Under a typical treaty tie-breaker, what is considered next?

choices.explanation: Correct. Personal and economic ties come next.

mcqs.explanation: Typical treaty tie-breakers: permanent home, center of vital interests, habitual abode, nationality, then mutual agreement.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation (21% rate) has $1,000,000 of foreign general income taxed abroad at 15% and $200,000 of foreign passive income taxed at 30%. What foreign tax credit is allowed?

choices.explanation: Excess passive taxes can't use general room.
Passive credits are allowed up to their limit.

mcqs.explanation: FTC limits are computed separately; the $18,000 passive excess can't offset general-category limitation room.

mcqs.stem: What makes a foreign corporation a controlled foreign corporation?

choices.explanation: Correct. Each counts only at 10% or more.

mcqs.explanation: A CFC is more than 50% owned, by vote or value, by U.S. shareholders who each own at least 10%.

mcqs.stem: Which form reports a U.S. person's interest in certain foreign corporations?
mcqs.explanation: Form 5471 reports ownership of and transactions with certain foreign corporations.

mcqs.stem: Above what aggregate balance must a U.S. person file an FBAR?

choices.explanation: Correct. At any time during the year.

mcqs.explanation: An FBAR is required if aggregate foreign account balances exceed $10,000 at any time during the year.

mcqs.stem: A foreign corporation is owned 30% by U.S. person A, 15% by U.S. person B, 8% by U.S. person C and 47% by foreign persons. Is it a CFC?

choices.text: Yes; A and B control it

mcqs.explanation: Only U.S. shareholders owning 10% or more count toward the 50% test.

mcqs.stem: A CFC earns $200,000 of foreign personal holding company income. A U.S. shareholder owns 60%. What is her Subpart F inclusion?
mcqs.explanation: U.S. shareholders include their pro rata share of a CFC's Subpart F income currently.

mcqs.stem: A CFC has $30,000,000 of gross income, including $800,000 of foreign base company income. What is Subpart F income?

choices.explanation: Correct. Below the lesser of 5% or $1 million.

mcqs.explanation: If foreign base company income is below the lesser of 5% of gross income or $1 million, none is Subpart F income.

mcqs.stem: A CFC's income is taxed abroad at a 20% effective rate. What exception may apply?
mcqs.explanation: Income taxed above 90% of the U.S. corporate rate may be excluded by election.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation owning 40% of a foreign corporation for 2 years receives a $1,000,000 foreign-source dividend. What deduction applies?
mcqs.explanation: §245A allows a 100% DRD for the foreign-source portion of dividends from 10%-owned foreign corporations.

mcqs.stem: Foreign-source taxable income is $300,000 of $1,000,000 worldwide. U.S. tax before credits is $210,000, and foreign taxes paid are $80,000. What credit is allowed?

choices.explanation: Correct. Limited by the FTC limitation.

mcqs.explanation: The FTC is limited to U.S. tax × foreign-source ÷ worldwide income; excess carries back 1 and forward 10 years.

mcqs.stem: A qualifying expatriate earns $150,000 of foreign wages in 2025. What is the maximum foreign earned income exclusion?
mcqs.explanation: For 2025, up to $130,000 of foreign earned income may be excluded.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. citizen worked abroad 300 full days in a 12-month period and has no foreign residence. Does she meet the physical presence test?
mcqs.explanation: The physical presence test requires 330 full days in a foreign country in 12 consecutive months.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation operates abroad through a branch. When is the branch's income taxed in the U.S.?
mcqs.explanation: Foreign branch income is part of the U.S. corporation's taxable income as earned.

mcqs.stem: In 2025, a C corporation has a $1,000,000 GILTI inclusion before the §250 deduction. What is the U.S. tax before credits?
mcqs.explanation: For 2025, corporations deduct 50% of GILTI, for an effective 10.5% rate before credits.

mcqs.stem: In 2025, a C corporation has $400,000 of FDII. What §250 deduction applies?
mcqs.explanation: For 2025, the FDII deduction is 37.5%, for an effective 13.125% rate.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation pays a $100,000 dividend to a foreign shareholder with no treaty. What must it withhold?
mcqs.explanation: U.S.-source FDAP income paid to foreign persons is subject to 30% withholding unless reduced by treaty.

mcqs.stem: The same $100,000 dividend goes to a resident of a treaty country with a 15% dividend rate. What is withheld?
mcqs.explanation: Treaty rates reduce statutory withholding when the recipient qualifies.

mcqs.stem: A foreign person sells U.S. real property for $1,000,000. What FIRPTA withholding generally applies?
mcqs.explanation: Buyers generally withhold 15% of the amount realized from foreign sellers of U.S. real property.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. parent sells goods to its foreign subsidiary at artificially low prices. What can the IRS do?
mcqs.explanation: §482 lets the IRS reallocate income between related parties to reflect arm's-length pricing.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. company expects early losses from a new foreign operation. Which structure lets it use the losses now?

choices.explanation: Correct. Losses flow into U.S. income.

mcqs.explanation: Branch losses offset U.S. income currently; subsidiary losses generally don't.

mcqs.stem: A CFC earns mostly active business income in a low-tax country. Which regime is most likely to tax it currently?
mcqs.explanation: GILTI reaches low-taxed active CFC income that isn't Subpart F income.

mcqs.stem: A corporation has excess foreign tax credits every year. What may help it use them?
mcqs.explanation: Increasing foreign-source income within the right basket raises the FTC limitation.

mcqs.stem: An expatriate works in a country with higher income tax rates than the U.S. Which approach usually works best?

choices.explanation: Correct. High foreign taxes offset U.S. tax.

mcqs.explanation: In high-tax countries, the FTC can offset U.S. tax on all foreign income.

mcqs.stem: A foreign company wants reduced U.S. withholding under a treaty. What must it show?
mcqs.explanation: Treaty benefits require residence and meeting any limitation-on-benefits article.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation owning 30% of a foreign subsidiary wants to bring cash home. What is the federal tax effect of a dividend?

choices.explanation: Correct. Holding period must be met.

mcqs.explanation: Foreign-source dividends from 10%-owned foreign corporations are generally exempt under §245A.

mcqs.stem: A foreign investor plans to buy U.S. rental property. What should she plan for at sale?
mcqs.explanation: Foreign sellers of U.S. real property face FIRPTA tax and withholding.

mcqs.stem: A U.S. corporation's pre-credit U.S. tax is $210,000 on worldwide taxable income of $1,000,000, including $200,000 of foreign-source taxable income on which it paid $50,000 of foreign tax. What is its foreign tax credit?

choices.explanation: Correct. Limitation = 210,000 × 200,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 42,000, less than the 50,000 paid.
That is the excess credit, not the credit.
The limitation uses the foreign share of income.

mcqs.explanation: IRC §904: the foreign tax credit is limited to U.S. tax × foreign-source taxable income ÷ worldwide taxable income; excess credits carry back 1 and forward 10 years.

mcqs.stem: A foreign corporation is a controlled foreign corporation when U.S. shareholders — each owning at least 10% — together own:

choices.text: At least 25% of its vote and value
More than 50% of its vote or value
choices.explanation: Correct. That is the CFC test.

choices.text: Any shares listed on a U.S. exchange

mcqs.explanation: IRC §957(a), §951(b): a CFC is more than 50% owned (vote or value) by U.S. shareholders, each owning at least 10%.

flashcards.back: Residence of the payer (a domestic payer = U.S. source).

flashcards.front: FDAP income of a foreign person
flashcards.back: 30% of the gross amount, collected by withholding, unless a treaty reduces it.
A fixed place of business or a dependent agent that habitually concludes contracts; business profits are taxable in the source country only if attributable to one.
More than 50% of vote or value owned by U.S. shareholders, each owning at least 10%.
U.S. tax × foreign-source taxable income ÷ worldwide taxable income; excess back 1, forward 10.
